title: The Vilna Gaon
hook: a great scholar of Talmud who opposed the new Hasidic movement

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hasidism spread from the Maggid's students to the rebbes' tables. Your line was joy spreads. Today the week ends with the man who stood against that movement.

In Vilna, behind closed shutters, a lamp burns in the daytime. Inside, a man sits with a page of Talmud; the stories say he kept the shutters shut so the street would not pull at his attention. He held no grand office. Yet letters came from far away, questions from rabbis who wanted his judgment, and people in the city spoke his name with a kind of awe. They gave him a title that means genius. Today, his name.
screen: `SHUTTERS CLOSED IN DAYLIGHT.` → `NO GRAND OFFICE.` → `A TITLE THAT MEANS GENIUS.`

segments.voice: Rabbi Elijah son of Solomon Zalman is remembered as the Vilna Gaon. Gaon was once the title of the heads of the great academies in Babylonia; in his day it became a word of honor for an extraordinary mind. Tradition says he held no official post as a rabbi in Vilna. He studied, mostly alone, and wrote notes and commentaries across the Bible, the Mishnah, the Talmud, Jewish law and the Kabbalah. He studied grammar, mathematics and astronomy too, because, he taught, they help a person understand the Torah. He lived the verse from Joshua: "thou shalt meditate therein day and night." Then the Hasidic movement reached Lithuania. The Gaon saw danger in it: rebbes whom followers seemed to treat as more than human, prayers said at changed times and in new ways, joy and ecstasy he feared would push aside careful study. He backed bans against the Hasidim. Hasidic tradition tells that Rabbi Shneur Zalman came to Vilna hoping to speak with him, and the Gaon would not receive him. His followers came to be called Mitnagdim, the opponents, and the two sides argued for years, sometimes bitterly. Each, in its own way, guarded something it loved: for one, above all the joy of serving God; for the other, above all the discipline of learning. Hasidim studied too, and Mitnagdim prayed with feeling. This week: 1648, a false messiah, Luzzatto's ladder, a council at the fair, a healer in the forests, joy spreading, and now the genius of Vilna.
screen: `GAON: A WORD OF HONOR.` · `NO OFFICE, ONLY STUDY.` · `DAY AND NIGHT.` · `AGAINST THE NEW MOVEMENT.` · then, large: `THE GENIUS OF VILNA.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone whose learning has shaped you, a teacher, an author, a grandparent who knew the old stories, and think of the hours they spent at a table so you could understand faster. Hold them with gratitude, and if you disagree with them about something, hold that too; honor and disagreement can sit together. If you pray, you can give thanks for them in your own words.
Gaon. A word of honor for an extraordinary mind, the title people gave Rabbi Elijah of Vilna for his vast, mostly solitary learning. Today's word.
Your line: the genius of vilna. Two camps, each guarding something it loved. Week done; see you tomorrow.

howItsDone: The Vilna Gaon's notes are printed in the margins of standard editions of the Talmud and other texts, and Lithuanian-style yeshivas still regard him as a model of devoted study.
